title: Theil indices
text:
Definition
Let Y be a positive random variable with mean \mu = E[Y]. The Theil indices are members of the generalised entropy family GE(\alpha):

T_1 = GE(1) = E\left[\frac{Y}{\mu}\log\frac{Y}{\mu}\right],
\qquad
T_0 = GE(0) = E\left[\log\frac{\mu}{Y}\right] = \log\mu - E[\log Y].

T_1 is the Theil index and T_0 the mean logarithmic deviation (MLD). Both are zero under perfect equality and increase with inequality. T_1 is more sensitive to the upper tail of the distribution, and T_0 to the lower tail.

title: Theil indices
text:
Additive decomposition
If the population is partitioned into G groups with population shares p_g, income shares s_g, means \mu_g and indices T_{0g}, T_{1g}:

T_1 = \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} s_g\, T_{1g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} s_g \log\frac{\mu_g}{\mu}}_{\text{between}},
\qquad
T_0 = \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} p_g\, T_{0g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} p_g \log\frac{\mu}{\mu_g}}_{\text{between}}.

This property makes the Theil indices the standard tool to identify the sources of inequality: by region, gender, age, education, sector, type of employment or municipality size.

title: Theil indices
Theil indices
text:
Jackknife bias correction and variance
Let \widehat{T}_{(i)} be the estimator computed without observation i, and \widehat{T}_{(\cdot)} = n^{-1}\sum_i \widehat{T}_{(i)}. The jackknife bias-corrected estimator and variance estimator are

\widehat{T}^{\,J} = n\,\widehat{T} - (n-1)\,\widehat{T}_{(\cdot)},
\qquad
\widehat{V}_J = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\widehat{T}_{(i)} - \widehat{T}_{(\cdot)}\right)^2 .

The standard implementation recomputes the index n times, with cost O(n^2). Because \widehat{T}_0 and \widehat{T}_1 depend on the data only through a few sums, every leave-one-out value can be obtained by subtracting observation i from those sums, with cost O(n):
# Leave-one-out values in O(n)
T.loo <- function(y, index = c("T1", "T0")) {
  index <- match.arg(index)
  n  <- length(y)
  Sy <- sum(y)
  m.i <- (Sy - y) / (n - 1)                      # leave-one-out means
  if (index == "T1") {
    Sylogy <- sum(y * log(y))
    (Sylogy - y * log(y)) / (Sy - y) - log(m.i)
  } else {
    Slogy <- sum(log(y))
    log(m.i) - (Slogy - log(y)) / (n - 1)
  }
}

jackknife.theil <- function(y, index = c("T1", "T0")) {
  index <- match.arg(index)
  n   <- length(y)
  est <- if (index == "T1") T1.hat(y) else T0.hat(y)
  loo <- T.loo(y, index)
  m.loo <- mean(loo)
  list(estimate  = est,
       corrected = n * est - (n - 1) * m.loo,
       variance  = (n - 1) / n * sum((loo - m.loo)^2))   # two-pass
}
These functions will be part of the R package theil, developed in WP4.

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Introduction
This guide shows how to estimate Theil indices in R, how to decompose them into between-group and within-group components, and how to measure their bias and precision. All code uses base R or packages currently on CRAN.
The two Theil indices belong to the generalised entropy family GE(\alpha):

T_1 (Theil’s T index, GE(1)): more sensitive to the top of the distribution.
T_0 (mean log deviation, MLD, GE(0)): more sensitive to the bottom.

Both equal 0 under perfect equality, satisfy the Pigou–Dalton transfer principle, are scale invariant and, above all, are additively decomposable: total inequality is exactly the sum of a between-group part (regions, sex, sectors) and a within-group part. This property, which the Gini index lacks, is the main reason to use them.
The theil R package developed in THEILUMINA will bring estimation, bias correction and inference together in a single tool. Until then, this guide relies on existing functions.

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Formulas
Let y_1, \dots, y_n be positive incomes with sampling weights w_i and weighted mean \mu (unweighted: w_i = 1).

T_1 = \frac{\sum_i w_i \frac{y_i}{\mu}\ln\frac{y_i}{\mu}}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
T_0 = \frac{\sum_i w_i \ln\frac{\mu}{y_i}}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
\mu = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}

With G groups, where p_g is the population share of group g, \mu_g its mean and s_g = p_g \mu_g / \mu its income share:

T_1 = \underbrace{\sum_g s_g\, T_{1,g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_g s_g \ln\frac{\mu_g}{\mu}}_{\text{between}}, \qquad
T_0 = \underbrace{\sum_g p_g\, T_{0,g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_g p_g \ln\frac{\mu}{\mu_g}}_{\text{between}}

In T_1, within-group inequality is weighted by income shares; in T_0, by population shares. This is why T_0 is preferred when every person should count equally, and why it is the only index whose between-group term does not depend on within-group inequality.
Both indices require strictly positive incomes, since logarithms are undefined for zero or negative values.

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Estimation in R

Base R
Two short functions, with optional weights, are enough:
theil_T1 <- function(y, w = rep(1, length(y))) {
  stopifnot(all(y > 0))
  mu <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  r  <- y / mu
  sum(w * r * log(r)) / sum(w)
}

theil_T0 <- function(y, w = rep(1, length(y))) {
  stopifnot(all(y > 0))
  mu <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  sum(w * log(mu / y)) / sum(w)
}

y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80)
theil_T1(y)   # 0.1809
theil_T0(y)   # 0.2114

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Between- and within-group decomposition
In the example, two regions account for 72% of total inequality according to T_1 and 68% according to T_0. This function applies the formulas above to any grouping variable:
theil_decomp <- function(y, g, w = rep(1, length(y)), type = c("T1", "T0")) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  mu   <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  grp  <- split(seq_along(y), g)
  res  <- t(sapply(grp, function(i) {
    p   <- sum(w[i]) / sum(w)              # population share
    mug <- weighted.mean(y[i], w[i])       # group mean
    s   <- p * mug / mu                    # income share
    Tg  <- if (type == "T1") theil_T1(y[i], w[i]) else theil_T0(y[i], w[i])
    if (type == "T1") c(p = p, s = s, T_g = Tg, within = s * Tg, between = s * log(mug / mu))
    else              c(p = p, s = s, T_g = Tg, within = p * Tg, between = p * log(mu / mug))
  }))
  W <- sum(res[, "within"]); B <- sum(res[, "between"])
  list(groups  = res,
       summary = c(total = W + B, within = W, between = B, pct_between = 100 * B / (W + B)))
}

g <- c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B")
theil_decomp(y, g, type = "T1")$summary

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Full example: income by region
This example simulates log-normal incomes in four regions with different means and spreads, computes both indices, decomposes them and plots each region’s contribution. Exact values depend on the seed; what matters is the interpretation.
set.seed(2026)
regions <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "East", "West"),
  n      = c(400, 300, 200, 100),
  mean   = c(9.9, 9.5, 10.1, 9.7),   # mean of log(income)
  sd     = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.4)
)
data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(regions)), function(k) {
  with(regions[k, ], data.frame(region = region,
                                income = rlnorm(n, meanlog = mean, sdlog = sd)))
}))

# Overall indices
theil_T1(data$income)
theil_T0(data$income)

# Decomposition by region
dT0 <- theil_decomp(data$income, data$region, type = "T0")
round(dT0$groups, 4)
round(dT0$summary, 4)

# Each region's contribution to within-region inequality
library(ggplot2)
contrib <- data.frame(region = rownames(dT0$groups),
                      within = dT0$groups[, "within"])
ggplot(contrib, aes(reorder(region, within), within)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#E07B20") + coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribution to T0 (within regions)")
How to read the output:

pct_between is the share of inequality due to differences in regional mean incomes. Regional convergence policies can only act on this part.
The within column shows which regions contribute most internal inequality. It depends both on their own inequality (T_g) and on their size (p).
If T_1 and T_0 tell different stories, inequality is concentrated in different tails: T_1 reacts to the top and T_0 to the bottom.

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Bias and precision
Sample estimators of T_0 and T_1 are biased, usually downwards, and more so in small samples and with heavy-tailed distributions. They should therefore not be reported without a measure of precision. The jackknife gives both a bias estimate and a standard error:

\widehat{\text{bias}} = (n-1)\,(\bar T_{(\cdot)} - \hat T), \qquad
\tilde T = \hat T - \widehat{\text{bias}}, \qquad
\widehat{\text{Var}} = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i \big(\hat T_{(i)} - \bar T_{(\cdot)}\big)^2

Computing the n leave-one-out indices by repeating the formula costs \mathcal{O}(n^2). Because T_0 and T_1 depend only on a few sums, all of them can be obtained at once in \mathcal{O}(n) (THEILUMINA preliminary results; see Research problems), which makes the jackknife feasible with millions of observations:
jackknife_theil <- function(y, type = c("T1", "T0")) {
  type <- match.arg(type); n <- length(y)
  S1 <- sum(y); S2 <- sum(y * log(y)); L <- sum(log(y))
  if (type == "T1") {
    T    <- S2 / S1 - log(S1 / n)
    Tloo <- (S2 - y * log(y)) / (S1 - y) - log((S1 - y) / (n - 1))
  } else {
    T    <- log(S1 / n) - L / n
    Tloo <- log((S1 - y) / (n - 1)) - (L - log(y)) / (n - 1)
  }
  bias <- (n - 1) * (mean(Tloo) - T)
  se   <- sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((Tloo - mean(Tloo))^2))
  c(T = T, bias = bias, T_corrected = T - bias, se = se)
}

round(jackknife_theil(y, "T1"), 4)  # T 0.1809  bias -0.0296  T_corrected 0.2106  se 0.0858
round(jackknife_theil(y, "T0"), 4)  # T 0.2114  bias -0.0372  T_corrected 0.2486  se 0.1071
With only six observations the standard error is almost half the index: the example shows why a point value without a margin of error can mislead.
For confidence intervals the bootstrap is the usual alternative. With skewed distributions, bootstrap-t or BCa intervals are preferable to percentile intervals:
library(boot)
b <- boot(data$income, function(d, i) theil_T0(d[i]), R = 2000)
boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "bca"))
For survey data, convey::svygei() already returns linearisation standard errors that account for strata and clusters. THEILUMINA studies how to predict and correct the bias (GO1), build reliable intervals (GO2) and reduce the cost of the jackknife (GO3), and will bring it all together in the theil package (GO4).

title: A practical guide to Theil indices in R
text:
Common pitfalls and good practice

Mixing up T_0 and T_1. Always state which one you use and check the package convention (in ineq, parameter = 0 is T_1).
Zero or negative incomes. Logarithms fail, or packages drop them silently. Decide explicitly how to handle them (exclude, bottom-code, or use another GE index) and report how many there are.
Ignoring weights. With survey data, unweighted indices do not estimate population inequality.
Comparing without a margin of error. A difference between regions or years only matters if it exceeds the estimator’s uncertainty. Report each index with its standard error or confidence interval.
Over-disaggregating. Bias grows as groups get smaller. In decompositions with many small groups, correct the bias or merge categories.
Not checking the decomposition. Within + between must equal the total; if it does not, there is an error in the weights or the groups.

section: Parameters for a given value of the index
text:
Parameters for a given value of the index
The following functions return the parameter of each distribution that yields a given value of T_0 or T_1, using the closed forms on the page Theil indices.
# True Theil indices
T.lognormal <- function(sigma)       sigma^2 / 2
T.pareto    <- function(alpha, index) if (index == "T1")
  1 / (alpha - 1) - log(alpha / (alpha - 1)) else log(alpha / (alpha - 1)) - 1 / alpha
T.gamma     <- function(k, index) if (index == "T1")
  digamma(k) + 1 / k - log(k) else log(k) - digamma(k)

# Parameter giving a target value of the index
param.theil <- function(T, dist = c("lognormal", "pareto", "gamma"),
                        index = c("T0", "T1")) {
  dist  <- match.arg(dist)
  index <- match.arg(index)
  switch(dist,
    lognormal = sqrt(2 * T),
    pareto    = uniroot(function(a) T.pareto(a, index) - T, c(1 + 1e-6, 1e4))$root,
    gamma     = uniroot(function(k) T.gamma(k, index)  - T, c(1e-4, 1e5))$root)
}

RB.theil <- function(T, n, R = 1000, dist = "pareto", index = "T0") {

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Introducción
Esta guía muestra cómo estimar los índices de Theil en R, cómo descomponerlos entre grupos y dentro de ellos, y cómo medir su sesgo y su precisión. Todo el código usa R base o paquetes disponibles hoy en CRAN.
Los dos índices de Theil pertenecen a la familia de entropía generalizada GE(\alpha):

T_1 (índice de Theil T, GE(1)): es más sensible a lo que ocurre en la parte alta de la distribución.
T_0 (desviación logarítmica media o MLD, GE(0)): es más sensible a la parte baja.

Ambos valen 0 con igualdad perfecta, cumplen el principio de transferencias de Pigou-Dalton, no dependen de la escala de la renta y, sobre todo, son aditivamente descomponibles. La desigualdad total es exactamente la suma de una parte entre grupos (regiones, sexo, sectores) y otra dentro de ellos. Esta propiedad, que el índice de Gini no tiene, es la razón principal para usarlos.
El paquete de R theil de THEILUMINA reunirá en una sola herramienta la estimación, la corrección del sesgo y la inferencia. Mientras tanto, esta guía usa las funciones que ya existen.

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Fórmulas
Sea una muestra de rentas positivas y_1, \dots, y_n con pesos muestrales w_i y media ponderada \mu. Sin pesos, basta con tomar w_i = 1.

T_1 = \frac{\sum_i w_i \frac{y_i}{\mu}\ln\frac{y_i}{\mu}}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
T_0 = \frac{\sum_i w_i \ln\frac{\mu}{y_i}}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
\mu = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}

Con G grupos, donde p_g es la proporción de población del grupo g, \mu_g su media y s_g = p_g \mu_g / \mu su proporción de renta, las descomposiciones son:

T_1 = \underbrace{\sum_g s_g\, T_{1,g}}_{\text{dentro}} + \underbrace{\sum_g s_g \ln\frac{\mu_g}{\mu}}_{\text{entre}}, \qquad
T_0 = \underbrace{\sum_g p_g\, T_{0,g}}_{\text{dentro}} + \underbrace{\sum_g p_g \ln\frac{\mu}{\mu_g}}_{\text{entre}}

En T_1 la desigualdad dentro de cada grupo se pondera por su peso en la renta; en T_0, por su peso en la población. Por eso T_0 es el índice preferido cuando se quiere que cada persona cuente lo mismo, y la única descomposición en la que la parte «entre» no depende de la desigualdad dentro de los grupos.
Ambos índices requieren rentas estrictamente positivas: los logaritmos no admiten ceros ni valores negativos.

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Estimación en R

Con R base
Dos funciones de pocas líneas bastan, con pesos opcionales:
theil_T1 <- function(y, w = rep(1, length(y))) {
  stopifnot(all(y > 0))
  mu <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  r  <- y / mu
  sum(w * r * log(r)) / sum(w)
}

theil_T0 <- function(y, w = rep(1, length(y))) {
  stopifnot(all(y > 0))
  mu <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  sum(w * log(mu / y)) / sum(w)
}

Con datos de encuesta (ECV/EU-SILC), convey es la opción más completa, porque tiene en cuenta el diseño muestral al calcular los errores estándar:
library(survey); library(convey)
des <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~estrato, weights = ~peso, data = ecv)
des <- convey_prep(des)

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
section: Descomposición entre y dentro de grupos
text:
Descomposición entre y dentro de grupos
En el ejemplo, dos regiones explican el 72 % de la desigualdad total según T_1 y el 68 % según T_0. Esta función aplica las fórmulas anteriores a cualquier variable de grupo:
theil_decomp <- function(y, g, w = rep(1, length(y)), tipo = c("T1", "T0")) {
  tipo <- match.arg(tipo)
  mu  <- weighted.mean(y, w)
  grp <- split(seq_along(y), g)
  res <- t(sapply(grp, function(i) {
    p   <- sum(w[i]) / sum(w)              # proporción de población
    mug <- weighted.mean(y[i], w[i])       # media del grupo
    s   <- p * mug / mu                    # proporción de renta
    Tg  <- if (tipo == "T1") theil_T1(y[i], w[i]) else theil_T0(y[i], w[i])
    if (tipo == "T1") c(p = p, s = s, T_g = Tg, dentro = s * Tg, entre = s * log(mug / mu))
    else              c(p = p, s = s, T_g = Tg, dentro = p * Tg, entre = p * log(mu / mug))
  }))
  W <- sum(res[, "dentro"]); B <- sum(res[, "entre"])
  list(grupos = res,
       resumen = c(total = W + B, dentro = W, entre = B, pct_entre = 100 * B / (W + B)))
}

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Ejemplo completo: renta por regiones
Este ejemplo simula rentas log-normales en cuatro regiones con medias y dispersiones distintas, calcula los dos índices, los descompone y representa la contribución de cada región. Los valores exactos dependen de la semilla; lo que importa es la interpretación.
set.seed(2026)
regiones <- data.frame(
  region = c("Norte", "Sur", "Este", "Oeste"),
  n      = c(400, 300, 200, 100),
  media  = c(9.9, 9.5, 10.1, 9.7),   # media de log(renta)
  sd     = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.4)
)
datos <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(regiones)), function(k) {
  with(regiones[k, ], data.frame(region = region,
                                 renta  = rlnorm(n, meanlog = media, sdlog = sd)))
}))

# Índices globales
theil_T1(datos$renta)
theil_T0(datos$renta)

# Descomposición por región
dT0 <- theil_decomp(datos$renta, datos$region, tipo = "T0")
round(dT0$grupos, 4)
round(dT0$resumen, 4)

# Contribución de cada región a la desigualdad "dentro"
library(ggplot2)
contrib <- data.frame(region = rownames(dT0$grupos),
                      dentro = dT0$grupos[, "dentro"])
ggplot(contrib, aes(reorder(region, dentro), dentro)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#E07B20") + coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribución a T0 (dentro de regiones)")
Cómo leer el resultado:

pct_entre indica qué parte de la desigualdad se debe a que las regiones tienen rentas medias distintas. Una política de convergencia regional solo puede actuar sobre esa parte.
La columna dentro muestra qué regiones aportan más desigualdad interna. Depende tanto de su desigualdad propia (T_g) como de su tamaño (p).
Si T_1 y T_0 dan mensajes distintos, la desigualdad se concentra en colas diferentes: T_1 reacciona a la parte alta y T_0 a la parte baja.

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R

La parte entre mide cuánta desigualdad desaparecería si mujeres y hombres tuvieran la misma renta media. Es la medida de la brecha de género que ofrecen los índices de Theil.

Con datos de encuesta, la misma descomposición con su error estándar se obtiene con convey::svygeidec(~renta, ~sexo, des, epsilon = 0). Es lo que permite decir si la brecha ha cambiado de verdad entre dos años.

La variable de grupo puede ser cualquier otra: discapacidad, nacionalidad, nivel educativo, o cruces como sexo × región (interaction(sexo, region)). Cuantos más grupos, más pequeños son y mayor es el sesgo, como se explica en la sección siguiente.

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Sesgo y precisión
Los estimadores muestrales de T_0 y T_1 tienen sesgo, que suele ser a la baja y es mayor en muestras pequeñas y con distribuciones de cola pesada. Por eso no deberían publicarse sin una medida de su precisión. El jackknife da a la vez una estimación del sesgo y del error estándar:

\widehat{\text{sesgo}} = (n-1)\,(\bar T_{(\cdot)} - \hat T), \qquad
\tilde T = \hat T - \widehat{\text{sesgo}}, \qquad
\widehat{\text{Var}} = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i \big(\hat T_{(i)} - \bar T_{(\cdot)}\big)^2

Calcular los n índices «dejando uno fuera» repitiendo la fórmula cuesta \mathcal{O}(n^2). Como T_0 y T_1 solo dependen de unas pocas sumas, todos se obtienen a la vez en \mathcal{O}(n) (resultados preliminares de THEILUMINA; véase Research problems), lo que hace el jackknife viable con millones de observaciones:
jackknife_theil <- function(y, tipo = c("T1", "T0")) {
  tipo <- match.arg(tipo); n <- length(y)
  S1 <- sum(y); S2 <- sum(y * log(y)); L <- sum(log(y))
  if (tipo == "T1") {
    T    <- S2 / S1 - log(S1 / n)
    Tloo <- (S2 - y * log(y)) / (S1 - y) - log((S1 - y) / (n - 1))
  } else {
    T    <- log(S1 / n) - L / n
    Tloo <- log((S1 - y) / (n - 1)) - (L - log(y)) / (n - 1)
  }
  sesgo <- (n - 1) * (mean(Tloo) - T)
  ee    <- sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((Tloo - mean(Tloo))^2))
  c(T = T, sesgo = sesgo, T_corregido = T - sesgo, ee = ee)
}

round(jackknife_theil(y, "T1"), 4)  # T 0.1809  sesgo -0.0296  T_corregido 0.2106  ee 0.0858
round(jackknife_theil(y, "T0"), 4)  # T 0.2114  sesgo -0.0372  T_corregido 0.2486  ee 0.1071
Con solo seis observaciones, el error estándar es casi la mitad del índice: el ejemplo muestra por qué un valor puntual sin margen de error puede engañar.
Para intervalos de confianza, el bootstrap es la alternativa habitual. Con distribuciones asimétricas conviene usar el intervalo bootstrap-t o el BCa, mejor que el de percentiles:
library(boot)
b <- boot(datos$renta, function(d, i) theil_T0(d[i]), R = 2000)
boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "bca"))
Con datos de encuesta, convey::svygei() ya devuelve el error estándar por linealización, teniendo en cuenta estratos y conglomerados. THEILUMINA estudia cómo predecir y corregir el sesgo (OG1), cómo construir intervalos fiables (OG2) y cómo reducir el coste del jackknife (OG3), y lo integrará todo en el paquete theil (OG4).

title: Guía práctica: índices de Theil en R
text:
Errores frecuentes y buenas prácticas

Confundir T_0 y T_1. Indica siempre cuál usas y comprueba la convención del paquete (en ineq, parameter = 0 es T_1).
Rentas nulas o negativas. Los logaritmos fallan o los paquetes las eliminan en silencio. Decide explícitamente qué hacer con ellas (excluirlas, acotarlas o usar otro índice de la familia GE) e informa de cuántas hay.
Olvidar los pesos. Con datos de encuesta, los índices sin ponderar no estiman la desigualdad de la población.
Comparar sin margen de error. Una diferencia entre regiones o años solo es relevante si supera la incertidumbre del estimador. Acompaña cada índice de su error estándar o de su intervalo de confianza.
Desagregar demasiado. El sesgo crece al reducirse el tamaño de cada grupo. En descomposiciones con muchos grupos pequeños, corrige el sesgo o agrupa categorías.
No verificar la descomposición. Dentro + entre debe coincidir con el total; si no coincide, hay un error en los pesos o en los grupos.

WP1 · Bias diagnosis and correction

title: Research problems and questions
text: Theil indices (T_0 and T_1) are the standard tool to decompose inequality into a between-group and a within-group component. Yet the way they are usually estimated and used in practice raises several problems that the project addresses. The figures on this page are preliminary results of the team, and illustrate the problems with the most skewed distribution considered (Pareto).

title: Research problems and questions
text:
Problem 1 · The estimators underestimate inequality
The standard (plug-in) estimators of the Theil indices are biased downwards in finite samples: they systematically underestimate inequality. The bias grows with the skewness of the data and the level of inequality, which are precisely the conditions found in income, wealth, water consumption or tourism data. With highly skewed data and high inequality, samples larger than 5,000 observations are needed for the bias to become negligible.



Relative bias of the standard, jackknife bias-corrected and semiparametric estimators of T_0 (left) and T_1 (right) for samples drawn from a Pareto distribution (high skewness). The standard estimator (solid blue) shows a negative bias that reaches about −20% with small samples and high inequality; the bias-corrected estimator (dashed green) stays close to zero; the semiparametric estimator can overestimate severely (values shown as text). Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP1)

RQ1. How large is the bias of the estimators of T_0 and T_1, and which data features (sample size, skewness, inequality, tails) drive it?
RQ2. Can the bias be predicted from observable sample features, so that users know in advance whether their estimate is reliable (negligible, mild, moderate or severe bias)?
RQ3. Which correction (jackknife, model-based, analytical or semiparametric) best reduces the bias without inflating the mean squared error?
RQ4. How does the bias propagate to the between- and within-group components of the decomposition?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 2 · Inference is unreliable: variances are underestimated
text:
Problem 2 · Inference is unreliable: variances are underestimated
Even when the point estimate is acceptable, its margin of error may not be. Under skewed distributions, the usual asymptotic and bootstrap variance estimators severely underestimate the true variance (by 30–70% in the figure below), even with thousands of observations. As a result, confidence intervals are too narrow and differences in inequality across regions, groups or years may be declared significant when they are not. The jackknife variance estimator remains close to the region of negligible bias.



Relative bias of the asymptotic (solid blue), jackknife (dashed green) and bootstrap (dash-dotted red) variance estimators of the Theil indices for samples drawn from a Pareto distribution. Dashed black lines at ±5% delimit the region of negligible bias, and orange lines at ±20% the region of severe bias. Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP2)

RQ5. Under which combinations of sample size, skewness and inequality do the asymptotic, bootstrap, semiparametric and jackknife variance estimators become unreliable?
RQ6. Can new jackknife-based variance estimators and confidence intervals achieve coverage close to the nominal level under strong skewness and inequality, both for the indices and for their decomposition?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 3 · The jackknife is computationally prohibitive
text:
Problem 3 · The jackknife is computationally prohibitive
The jackknife recomputes the estimator n times, leaving out one observation each time, so its cost grows quadratically with the sample size (\mathcal{O}(n^2)). With n = 100{,}000 observations, the standard jackknife needs more than 16 minutes to compute the variance of a single Theil index, and a Monte Carlo study with n = 5{,}000 takes more than two days. Our closed-form expressions give exactly the same result with linear cost (\mathcal{O}(n)): 15 milliseconds and less than 40 seconds, respectively. For the bias-corrected estimators, the standard jackknife would take decades, which makes reduced expressions essential.



Computation times, in R, of the standard jackknife, the proposed closed-form jackknife and the asymptotic variance estimators of T_0 and T_1. Top: large samples (n up to 100,000). Bottom: complete Monte Carlo experiment (48,000 samples per sample size). Note the change of units: minutes and days for the standard jackknife, seconds for the proposed expressions. Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP3)

RQ7. How large is the computational cost of the standard jackknife compared with alternative variance estimators for big data (surveys and administrative records with millions of observations)?
RQ8. Can exact, closed-form jackknife expressions be derived for the bias-corrected estimators, the decomposition components and complex survey designs, with no loss of accuracy?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 4 · There is no open software for reliable Theil inference
text:
Problem 4 · There is no open software for reliable Theil inference
Existing software computes point estimates of Theil indices and, at most, bootstrap or linearisation standard errors (for example, the R packages convey and inequality). None offers bias diagnostics or bias corrections, jackknife variance estimators, or inference that remains reliable under strong skewness and scales to large samples.

Research question (WP4)

RQ9. Can the methods developed in WP1–WP3 be implemented in an open, documented and efficient R package (theil, with a C++ core) that makes reliable inference for Theil indices accessible to applied researchers?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 5 · Do corrected estimates change empirical conclusions?
text:
Problem 5 · Do corrected estimates change empirical conclusions?
The bias is not a technicality. When the methods are applied to real data, the difference between standard and bias-corrected estimates varies with sample size, skewness and inequality, and can change rankings and conclusions. For example, in our application to real GDP per capita for 183 countries (1990–2023), the bias-corrected estimates are between 2% and 6% higher for T_0, and up to 12% higher for T_1, than the standard ones, with the largest differences in the most skewed regions (the Americas and Asia & Pacific).

Research questions (WP5)

RQ10. How unequal are household water consumption and expenditure between and within municipalities, and how much does the bias correction change this picture?
RQ11. Does tourism reduce or increase income inequality within and between destinations?
RQ12. How unequal are servitization, digital transformation and AI adoption across firms, sectors and countries?
RQ13. Is there global convergence in per capita consumption and income once bias-corrected estimators and reliable confidence intervals are used?


See Objectives, work packages and activities for how these questions are organised into work packages.
